meta.scope: Applying for NSHD data, what happens after approval, and finding variables. Answers come from the OWL Data Sharing pages (Apply for Data and its sub-pages) and the OWL search and documentation pages.

entries.question: How do I apply for NSHD data?
entries.keywords: apply application how to get data request start begin steps process requesting access request access apply for data diagram flowchart stages overview
entries.answer:
Each application is for one project and a set of variables. The steps are:

  1. Explore the variables on OWL, then build a basket in Condor. You get a basket ID.
  2. Make sure your Condor basket holds all the variables you need. You can add them one at a time, or upload a completed data dictionary in Condor to build the basket for you. Completing the spreadsheet is optional.
  3. Submit the Data Access Request Form. You can include your basket ID, or send it any time after your project is approved.
  4. The Science Support Team reviews your request and the Data Sharing Committee decides. This takes 30 days at most, usually about two weeks.
  5. If approved, you are emailed for the prerequisites, invited to Information Governance training, and your secure share and Data Safe Haven account are set up.
  6. You get access to your data in the UCL Data Safe Haven.

entries.question: What do I need before I apply?
entries.keywords: prerequisite prerequisites before need require requirements eligible eligibility ready criteria ethics ethical approval training agreement agreements governance first
entries.answer:
Have a defined project, the list of variables you need, and your basket. Four things must also be completed before you can be given access. You do not attach them to your application: you are emailed for each one as it progresses.

  • Data Security Awareness Training, renewed every 12 months.
  • UCL Data Safe Haven access: a signed Approved Researcher Agreement and your contact details.
  • Confidentiality Form, on your first application only. Every applicant must return one.
  • Data Sharing Agreement, only if your institution has not shared data with NSHD before.

entries.question: What is the data dictionary and do I have to complete one?
entries.keywords: data dictionary spreadsheet excel mark y request variable column complete fill download template upload condor basket optional required need
entries.answer:
The data dictionary is an Excel spreadsheet listing NSHD variables. You mark Y against each variable you want in the "Request variable" column.

You do not have to complete one. What you do need is a Condor basket holding your variables, and its basket ID. The spreadsheet is there to make that easy: you can upload your completed data dictionary in Condor and it builds the basket for you, instead of adding variables one at a time.

You can fill it in by hand, or build a basket on OWL and download a copy that is already marked for you.

entries.question: How do I find the variables I need?
entries.keywords: find choose select search browse variables variable explore look ways methods searches different options overview
entries.answer:
There are several ways to search for variables, depending on where you want to start:

  • Search Data Dictionary: search variable names and labels by keyword.
  • Browse by Category: follow topics and subtopics.
  • Search by Year: start from the year or sweep a variable was collected.
  • Popular variables: a starting list of frequently requested variables.
  • Longitudinal search: variables measured the same way across two or more sweeps.
  • Search Documentation: write-ups and data notes about variables and datasets.
  • Discover Projects: what approved projects have asked for.
  • UK LLC Catalogue: the NSHD datasets deposited into UK LLC.

Add any variable to your basket from the results.

entries.question: What happens after I submit?
entries.keywords: after submit submitted happens next process review committee approved approval stages reviews reviewed reviewer who decides decision assess assessed confidentiality sign agreement stages confirmation email received secure share
entries.answer:
1. You are emailed to confirm your request has been received. If you have heard nothing within 10 working days, contact the team.
  2. The Science Support Team reviews your request and basket.
  3. The Data Sharing Committee decides: approved, or more information needed. A decision takes 30 days at most, usually about two weeks. You are emailed if there is a delay.
  4. If approved, you are emailed for your prerequisites, the Data Safe Haven team invites you to Information Governance training, and the Science Support Team sets up your secure share and requests your Data Safe Haven account.
  5. You then get access to your data in the UCL Data Safe Haven.

entries.question: How long does it take?
entries.keywords: long time take weeks months days turnaround wait waiting timescale duration soon quickly speed quickly processed processing fast speed decision approval maximum 30 days two weeks month confirmation
entries.answer:
• Confirmation: you are emailed to say your request was received. If you have heard nothing within 10 working days, contact the team.
  • Decision: 30 days at most, and usually about two weeks, depending on committee meeting dates. You are emailed if there is a delay.
  • Data: once you are approved and the prerequisites are complete, data are typically received within about a month.

Requests for many variables take longer, because they need a more thorough risk assessment. Later baskets within the same project may also be delayed if the queue is long.

entries.question: What is the difference between OWL and Condor?

entries.answer:
• OWL is where you discover variables, and where the forms and guidance for applying are. It is public and needs no registration.
  • Condor holds the full set of variables. It is where you finalise, save and share your basket, and it needs a registered account.

entries.question: Should I use Condor or UK LLC?

entries.answer:

entries.question: Who can apply for NSHD data?
entries.keywords: who can apply eligible eligibility bona fide researcher student students supervisor co-applicant institution organisation phd
entries.answer:
Applicants must be bona fide researchers at an MRC-recognised organisation, with the expertise the project needs. Students need a supervisor as co-applicant.

Proposals are also expected to stay within study members' consent and to pose no risk to the study's viability or reputation.

entries.question: What is a facilitated collaboration?
entries.keywords: facilitated collaboration collaborator sensitive data cause of death emigration cancer registration biomedical conditions extra
entries.answer:
Some requests are handled as a facilitated collaboration, which may come with extra conditions. Examples are sensitive data (such as cause and date of death, residential or emigration history, cancer registration or NHS Digital data), extensive biomedical data, data not yet through full quality assurance, and proposals needing a lot of study team time.

NHS Digital data is available through the NSHD to UCL researchers only. Everyone else can access it through UK LLC.

If you think your project may need a facilitated collaboration, mention it when you apply, or contact the team first.

entries.answer:
Everyone who will use the data needs a Data Safe Haven account. Two things are needed to set one up:

  • A mobile phone number or alternative email address, sent to the same address.

The Science Support Team requests the account for you after approval.

entries.question: Do I need approval before I publish a paper?

entries.answer:
Yes. Every paper that uses NSHD data, including Insight 46 and MyoFit 46 data, is reviewed by the NSHD Data Sharing Committee before it is submitted to a journal. The review checks that confidentiality is protected and that the paper will not bring the study into disrepute, and the committee may also give advice and feedback.

  2. Email it to mrclha.swiftinfo@ucl.ac.uk.
  3. Wait for approval, then submit your paper.

entries.answer:
It organises variables into a tree of categories and subcategories, so you can browse by topic instead of searching by name. Each category page lists its variables with their names and labels. A variable can belong to more than one category.

Some parent categories show few or no variables themselves, because the variables sit in their subcategories.
